title: Shrove Tuesday
hookLine: confess and use up the rich food before Lent: pancakes
last: A LIGHT TO LIGHTEN THE GENTILES.

cards: Eggs, butter, milk, a bag of flour, a bit of sugar. On one Tuesday a year, in kitchens across Britain, Ireland and plenty of other places, it all goes into one bowl and comes out as a stack of pancakes.

Lemon and sugar for some, syrup for others, and a flip that lands on the floor at least once. In New Orleans the same day is Mardi Gras, French for fat Tuesday, with parades. It looks like a party, and it is.
But the old English name for the day isn't about food. It's about the other thing people did before Lent: they went to church and told the truth about themselves. Today's word is shrove.

teach.h: TO SHRIVE: TO HEAR AND FORGIVE.
teach.b: To shrive is an old English verb: to hear someone's confession and declare them forgiven. Shrove is its old past form, and shriven is what you are afterward: confessed, and let go.
So Shrove Tuesday was the day you got shriven, cleared out before Lent began the next morning with Ash Wednesday.

teach.h: CONFESS YOUR FAULTS ONE TO ANOTHER.
teach.b: The letter of James puts it plainly, in the King James Bible: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." Notice the direction.
One to another: not only up to God, but across, to a person. And the reason given isn't shame. It's healing.
Churches practice this differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians have the sacrament of confession with a priest. Anglicans offer it, and some use it.
Some Protestant churches confess together, out loud, in a shared prayer, or between friends. Then the pancakes.
Lent was traditionally a time of fasting from rich foods, and in some places that meant eggs, butter and milk. A kitchen full of them would spoil, or tempt.
So you used them up, cooked everything rich in the house and fed everyone you could.

teach.h: EMPTY THE HEART, THEN THE PANTRY.
teach.b: Put the two halves together: empty the heart, then empty the pantry. Say what's wrong, then sit down and eat with the people who know. The feast comes after the truth is told.

how: On the Tuesday before Ash Wednesday, families and churches in Britain, Ireland and elsewhere make pancakes, and some parishes hold pancake suppers or races; in other places the same day is kept as Mardi Gras or Carnival.

s: Shrove Tuesday is named after pancakes
the name comes from shrive: to hear a confession and forgive.
the letter of James tells Christians to confess their faults to one another
"Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed."
the Bible sets out the pancake custom
the custom grew from the Lenten fast from rich foods; the Bible doesn't mention it.

games.q: it's the night before the fast. your kitchen is full of eggs, butter and milk you won't be eating for weeks. what do you do?
o: hide them at the back of the cold store.
throw them out so they can't tempt you.
cook them all up and feed everyone you can.
games.why: the custom is to use the rich food up, cooking pancakes and sharing them, so the fast begins with an empty pantry and a full table behind it.

practice: Ask yourself, gently, what you'd want to set down before a fresh start: not a list, one thing, like a sharp word or a promise you let slide.
Name it once, honestly, and if you pray, tell it to God plainly and ask to be let go of it. Then let your mind turn to the table, and to who you'd love to share a meal with.

wordCard.voice: Shrove. The old past form of shrive: to hear a confession and set someone free of it. The day before Lent, named for clearing out the heart.

orig.note: Greek: confess (to one another), from James 5:16, the verse behind today's teach.

carryVoice: Your line: shriven and fed. An old word with a stack of pancakes on top. Until tomorrow.
